title: Apple says it's tightening macOS privacy controls amid the rise of AI agents
content:
Amid the rapid rise in AI agents requesting “Full Disk Access” to your Mac, Apple says it is making changes to macOS to protect user privacy.
While the company hasn’t shared specifics, Apple says users should understand what it means to give an app such “extraordinary” access to their Mac.
In a blog post on its Developer website, Apple explains that the Full Disk Access permission in macOS is meant to “allow backup apps to function properly on the Mac.” However, Apple says that “some developers” are using the Full Disk Access setting in macOS in “ways that could put users at risk.”
“We give developers powerful APIs to build incredible capabilities into their apps for Apple products, backed by a set of controls designed to protect users’ private data. Full Disk Access largely sidesteps these controls in order to allow backup apps to function properly on the Mac. Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems—including files, mail, messages, and even browsing history—without users’ full knowledge and understanding. For communication apps, this can also compromise the privacy of the people users are communicating with.”
In response, Apple says it will “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”
The company hasn’t shared any additional details about these controls or the changes it plans. Nonetheless, it says that the rise of “increasingly capable and autonomous” AI agents necessitates a greater focus on privacy and security:
“Going forward, we will introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action. Addressing this is critical. As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially. We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy.”
Apple’s announcement today comes amid the increasing popularity of tools like Meta Muse and OpenAI’s Dots. These are always-on AI agents that request substantial access to your personal data, and we’ve already seen some horror stories about Meta Muse in particular.

report.summary: Apple is tightening macOS Full Disk Access controls after raising alarms that increasingly autonomous AI agents and other apps can expose all user data.
report.background: macOS Full Disk Access was designed to let backup apps read protected locations such as Mail, Messages, Safari history, and user files. In a Developer blog post, Apple says some developers now use that permission in risky ways, giving apps sweeping visibility without users fully understanding the trade-off. The warning lands as always-on AI agents like Meta Muse and OpenAI's Dots request broad access to personal data to act autonomously. Apple has not detailed the new controls or timing, but says the rise of increasingly capable and autonomous agents makes stronger privacy and security safeguards necessary.
key_points: Apple says macOS Full Disk Access is intended for backup apps, but some developers use it in risky ways. It can expose files, mail, messages, and browsing history without users fully understanding the grant. Apple calls this an "extraordinary" permission that largely sidesteps normal privacy protections.

Apple will introduce additional controls so only users who genuinely want to grant Full Disk Access can do so, via very explicit action. The company has not shared technical details, timelines, or which macOS version will include the changes, leaving developers and users guessing for now.

The immediate catalyst is AI agents. Always-on assistants like Meta Muse and OpenAI's Dots request deep system access to act autonomously. Apple warns that as agents become more capable, the risks of broad access grow substantially, and users must understand those risks before granting permission.

Apple notes communication apps with Full Disk Access can compromise the privacy of contacts, not just the user. That broadens the privacy debate beyond personal data to third parties whose messages may be read or analyzed by an agent. It also signals tighter platform scrutiny of AI agent permission models.
report.impact: Apple's move could set a precedent for how operating systems gate autonomous AI agents. Developers building agents that rely on reading local files, messages, or browser data may face more explicit consent prompts, entitlement reviews, or sandbox limits, forcing redesigns around user-mediated access. AI companies may need to adopt narrower APIs, on-device processing, or user-approved data connectors. For regular users, the change should make it harder for an app to quietly obtain sweeping access, but it may also add friction and confusing prompts when setting up agents. The broader signal: platform owners are treating agentic AI as a privacy risk, not just a productivity feature, and will likely demand stronger transparency and control.
report.tools: For users, Objective-See's free tools—LuLu, OverSight, and BlockBlock—plus Little Snitch help monitor app behavior. For developers, review Apple's Full Disk Access and privacy manifest documentation, and watch open-source entitlement and sandboxing references like Google's Santa. macOS beta release notes are worth tracking for new Full Disk Access controls.
